title: Phase Matters: Characterizing Heterogeneous Vision-Language Inference on a Mobile SoC
abstract: Recent phone-class mobile SoCs expose practical NPU execution paths for on-device vision-language model (VLM) inference, but developers still lack phase-level guidance for mapping VLM pipelines across heterogeneous backends. We present a hardware-in-the-loop characterization of VLM inference on the Qualcomm SM8750 (Snapdragon 8 Elite), covering phase throughput, cache-state effects, 100-run thermal stability, energy, heterogeneous CPU/NPU pipeline configurations, and visual-token-budget sensitivity. Using FastVLM-0.5B as an end-to-end case study, together with encoder-only measurements across four architecture families, we show that phase matters: NPU execution is highly phase-dependent, delivering 1.64× speedup for prefill but only 1.18×for decode, while vision encoders achieve 20–45× speedups over CPU. These gains translate into 10.47°C lower steady-state temperature and 2.52× lower energy, avoiding thermal throttling in always-on settings. Finally, we show that a four-step graph rewrite enables previously unsupported encoders, such as Phi-3.5-V, to reach the QNN path with up to 22× speedup, providing a practical porting recipe for mobile VLM deployment.

title: Fold-PIM: A Cost-Efficient LPDDR5-Based PIM for On-Device SLMs
abstract: The increasing demand for on-device AI applications has shifted focus to Small Language Models (SLMs) optimized for mobile environments. However, the limited memory bandwidth of LPDDR5-based systems presents significant challenges for efficiently executing memory-bound matrix-vector multiplication operations, a core component of SLM inference. In this paper, we propose Fold-PIM, an LPDDR5-based Processing-in-Memory (PIM) architecture designed to address these challenges. FoldPIM features a shared PU architecture that leverages subarray level parallelism while maintaining cost efficiency. Additionally, we introduce key techniques, including adaptive tiling for efficient GEMV operations across diverse matrix sizes, a transposed data layout to minimize buffer overhead, and a tailored protocol to reduce vector replacement latency. Our evaluation results demonstrate that Fold-PIM achieves up to 3.9× speedup of token generation time in SLM inference compared to the baseline system without PIM.

title: On-Device Generative AI for GDPR-Compliant Visual Monitoring: Natural Language Alerts from Local Object Detection
abstract: Visual monitoring systems that rely on cloud-based AI inference expose raw image data to external services, creating fundamental tensions with the data-minimisation principle of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). This paper presents a proof-of-concept privacy-by-design pipeline that resolves this tension by confining all inference entirely to the edge device. A YOLOv5n-seg model compiled for a Hailo-8L AI accelerator delivers real-time object detection on a Raspberry Pi 5, from which raw pixel buffers are immediately discarded after inference. A stateful trigger engine forwards minimal JSON event payloads to a locally hosted instance of Phi-3 Mini (3.8B parameters, Q4_0 quantisation), which synthesises one-to-two sentence natural-language alerts for a human operator. No image data crosses the network boundary at any point; only the generated text alert is transmitted. We describe the full system architecture and implementation, report measured inference latency and resource utilisation on the target hardware, and present representative generated alerts. The results demonstrate that combining a dedicated neural-network accelerator with an on-device large language model on a single-board computer is not only feasible but produces practically deployable, human-readable monitoring output while aligning with GDPR Art. 5(1)(c) by design.

title: Causal Topologies for Edge Computing: Intrinsic Efficiency and Deep Intelligence Beyond the Transformer Paradigm
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The dominant paradigm for on-device artificial intelligence — compressing large transformer-based language and vision models to fit within the memory, compute, and power constraints of edge hardware — achieves efficiency through architectural compromise. Quantisation, adapter layers, speculative decoding, and hybrid cloud offloading are engineering responses to a fundamental mismatch between the transformer's computational profile and the physical constraints of edge devices. We argue that this mismatch is not an engineering problem but an architectural one, and that its solution lies not in making transformers smaller but in deploying a qualitatively different computational structure: the causal topology. A causal topology is a directed acyclic graph of causal mechanisms — entities connected by weighted, directional relationships encoding causal strength, confidence, and conditionality. Reasoning over a causal topology — through spreading activation, do-calculus, counterfactual inference, and dynamic graph growth — requires sparse graph traversal operations whose computational cost is orders of magnitude lower than transformer inference, while providing qualitatively superior intelligence: interventional reasoning (Pearl's Rung 2) and counterfactual reasoning (Pearl's Rung 3) that transformer architectures, regardless of scale or compression, are structurally incapable of producing. We present the theoretical foundations of causal topologies as an edge computing primitive, characterise their computational profile relative to transformer-based on-device AI, and demonstrate how two algorithms — the Generative Hierarchy Algorithm (GHA) and the Sustainability Optimizer (SO) — extend causal topologies with dynamic self-growth and sustained intervention optimisation. We further propose a hybrid architecture combining a lightweight transformer for perceptual encoding with a causal topology for interventional reasoning, and identify the application domains — autonomous systems, financial crime detection, health monitoring, industrial IoT — where this combination produces capabilities that no current on-device AI strategy delivers.

title: Efficient Scheduling of Transformer Neural Network Computation for Edge-AI Deployment
venue: Genetic and Evolutionary Computation Conference Companion (GECCO Companion)
abstract: Transformer neural networks have gained popularity in recent years, demonstrating remarkable performance across many application domains. However, inference on resource-constrained embedded hardware remains challenging due to Transformers' substantial computational demands. We aim to address this problem by focusing on exploiting the inherent parallelism opportunities presented by the multi-head self attention operations of Transformers, to achieve a speedup in processing on embedded hardware. In this paper, we present an evolutionary-based scheduling approach for distribution and allocation of Transformer operations across systolic array-based hardware accelerators used for execution. Our methodology takes as input specifications of the Transformer workload and the target systolic array architecture and explores the large mapping space to identify an efficient plan of operation-to-array assignments. The plans are evaluated against a hardware-aware cost model, capturing the cost of computational cycles for a given operation and systolic array, with the objective to minimize the total sum across all operations. Through extensive experimental evaluations across diverse systolic array dimensions, we demonstrate that our evolutionary-based scheduler surpasses conventional heuristics and is able to find plans offering up to 33.8% average reduction in overall cycle count.

title: DevFormer: A Symmetric Transformer for Context-Aware Device Placement
abstract: In this paper, we present DevFormer, a novel transformer-based architecture for addressing the complex and computationally demanding problem of hardware design optimization. Despite the demonstrated efficacy of transformers in domains including natural language processing and computer vision, their use in hardware design has been limited by the scarcity of offline data. Our approach addresses this limitation by introducing strong inductive biases such as relative positional embeddings and action-permutation symmetricity that effectively capture the hardware context and enable efficient design optimization with limited offline data. We apply DevFoemer to the problem of decoupling capacitor placement and show that it outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both simulated and real hardware, leading to improved performances while reducing the number of components by more than $30\%$. Finally, we show that our approach achieves promising results in other offline contextual learning-based combinatorial optimization tasks.

title: Performance Analysis of a Modular Framework for Edge-Based Generative Conversational AI
abstract: This study presents a multi-tier framework for deploying multi-modal Conversational AI on edge devices, spanning from constrained ultra-low-power systems to high-performance edge workstations. Utilizing an automated model discovery process and a modular benchmarking testbed, the research demonstrates that real-time, fully edge AI execution is feasible through strategic model selection and hardware acceleration. Key outcomes from the performance analysis are as follows. Speech-to-Text: Fun-ASR-Nano achieved the highest transcription accuracy with a Word Error Rate of 0.026, while Moonshine Tiny was the most efficient, recording a Real-Time Factor of 0.036 on the CPU. Scaling up to the high-performance tier, Whisper Large-V3 Turbo demonstrated high speed and robustness on a dedicated GPU, achieving an RTF of 0.093. Language Modeling: The Qwen 2.5 (1.5B Instruct) model, optimized for the Intel edge NPU, delivered robust constrained edge performance with an average generation speed of 20.15 tokens per second and a high semantic accuracy score of 0.86. The non-transformer Liquid LFM-24B model showcased server-level reasoning capabilities on the high-performance edge, reaching an impressive 39.2 tokens per second when fully offloaded to a dedicated GPU, despite its massive VRAM requirements. Text-to-Speech: Piper TTS emerged as the most efficient model for constrained environments (RTF of 0.034). However, Kokoro TTS redefined high-fidelity zero-shot synthesis on the GPU tier, achieving a groundbreaking RTF of 0.024 and far outperforming larger autoregressive audio models like OuteTTS, which remained too slow for real-time use without significant acceleration. Hardware Acceleration and Energy Efficiency: The use of Intel OpenVINO 2026.0 for hardware offloading significantly reduced energy consumption; for example, Whisper Large-V3 Turbo’s energy per audio second dropped from 52.68 Joules on the CPU to just 3.24 Joules on the integrated GPU. Furthermore, dedicated GPU acceleration revealed a critical “race-to-sleep” paradigm, where higher peak wattage is offset by drastically reduced processing times. The study concludes by identifying two optimal cascaded pipelines: a constrained edge tier (Moonshine, Qwen 1.5B, Piper) running on a Khadas NUC (Khadas Technology, Shenzhen, China powered by an Intel processor (Intel Corporation, Santa Clara, CA, USA) maximizing energy efficiency, and a high-performance tier (Whisper V3 Turbo, Liquid LFM-24B, Kokoro) running on an NVIDIA 5060ti, delivering uncompromising accuracy and subsecond latency for privacy-preserving, advanced edge AI.

title: Design and Implementation of an Embedded AI-Driven Telemetry and Self-Reconfiguration Framework for High-Power Electrical Platform
abstract: High-power electrical platforms—such as those found in electric mobility, aerospace systems, and smart energy infrastructures—are increasingly demanding advanced, real-time diagnostic and recovery mechanisms to ensure safe and uninterrupted operation. Traditional telemetry systems and static fault handlers fall short in addressing modern requirements of autonomy, adaptability, and intelligence. This paper presents a unified embedded framework that combines lightweight Transformer-based AI inference engines with dynamic hardware reconfiguration on FPGA-SoC platforms to enable intelligent telemetry and autonomous self-recovery. The proposed architecture operates entirely at the edge, using sensor fusion and time-series data to detect anomalies, infer root causes, and autonomously reconfigure hard-ware or firmware in real time. Implemented on a 50kW motor-drive testbed, the system achieves 94% diagnostic accuracy and executes mitigation actions in under 10ms. Unlike cloud-dependent or rule-based systems, this edge-native design is scalable, energy-efficient, and resilient, making it suitable for future adaptive electrical infrastructures. This work marks a substantial advancement toward real-time self-healing in mission-critical power systems.

title: A real-time FPGA-based radiation noise suppression and detection method with comparative analysis against deep learning techniques
RapidNet: Multi-Level Dilated Convolution Based Mobile Backbone
venue: IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV)
abstract: Vision transformers (ViTs) have dominated computer vision in recent years. However, ViTs are computationally expensive and not well suited for mobile devices; this led to the prevalence of convolutional neural network (CNN) and ViT-based hybrid models for mobile vision applications. Recently, Vision GNN (ViG) and CNN hybrid models have also been proposed for mobile vision tasks. However, all of these methods remain slower compared to pure CNN-based models. In this work, we propose Multi-Level Dilated Convolutions to devise a purely CNN-based mobile backbone. Using Multi-Level Dilated Convolutions allows for a larger theoretical receptive field than standard convolutions. Different levels of dilation also allow for interactions between the short-range and long-range features in an image. Experiments show that our proposed model outperforms state-of-the-art (SOTA) mobile CNN, ViT, ViG, and hybrid architectures in terms of accuracy and/or speed on image classification, object detection, instance segmentation, and semantic segmentation. Our fastest model, RapidNet-Ti, achieves 76.3% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K with 0.9 ms inference latency on an iPhone 13 mini NPU, which is faster and more accurate than MobileNetV2×1.4 (74.7% top-1 with 1.0 ms latency). Our work shows that pure CNN architectures can beat SOTA hybrid and ViT models in terms of accuracy and speed when designed properly11Code: https://github.com/mmunir127/RapidNet-Official:

title: Blind Assistant Mobile Application Using Computer Vision and Natural Language Processing Algorithms
venue: Zimbabwe Conference of Information and Communication Technologies (ZCICT)
abstract: Visually impaired individuals encounter substantial difficulties in navigating their physical environments. This significantly limits their social participation and economic independence. The aim of the study was to develop a model that detects objects' in real time and provide auditory feedback. Two deep learning models were employed for object detection and language understanding, “You Only Look Once” (YOLO) algorithm and “Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers” (BERT) respectively. The dataset comprised of 2500 images per class for object detection, 25GB was for language model. Images were captured using Android smartphones camera. English speech recordings, influenced by local Masvingo dialects, were captured using smartphone microphones. The data was standardised, annotated, fine-tuned and pre-processed using locally sourced visual data and dialect-influenced speech for effective training of the YOLO and BERT algorithms. The object detection model, mean average precision was 87% and accuracy was of 85%. The detection scores obtained were 0.78 for persons, 0.71 for dogs, and 0.66 for chairs. These class-level variations reflected differences in object size and background, while dynamic confidence thresholding improved detection reliability. The BERT language model achieved 82% accuracy in dialect-influenced speech-to-text and intent interpretation. This showed the ability of language model to understand the local English dialects. Hardware-aware optimisation and model compression reduced inference latency from over 200 ms on a CPU-only setup to approximately 25 ms per frame. This enabled the effective real-time object detection performance. The combined GPU–NPU optimisation further reduced end-to-end latency below 1.5 seconds, enabling real-time object detection with immediate voice feedback.

title: TinyVLM: Zero-Shot Object Detection on Microcontrollers via Vision-Language Distillation with Matryoshka Embeddings
abstract: Zero-shot object detection enables recognising novel objects without task-specific training, but current approaches rely on large vision language models (VLMs) like CLIP that require hundreds of megabytes of memory - far exceeding the constraints of micro controller units (MCUs). We present TinyVLM, the first framework enabling zero-shot object detection on resource-constrained MCUs with less than 1MB of memory. Our approach introduces three key innovations: (1) a decoupled architecture that separates visual inference from text encoding, allowing precomputed class embeddings to be stored in flash memory; (2) Matryoshka distillation that trains nested embeddings at multiple dimensions (16-256), enabling flexible accuracy-memory trade-offs; and (3) quantized embedding storage that reduces class prototype memory by 4x with minimal accuracy loss. Trained on Conceptual Captions 3M (CC3M), TinyVLM achieves competitive zero-shot accuracy on COCO, Flowers102, and Food101 while requiring only 285KB of RAM and 892KB of flash memory for the deployed vision encoder. We demonstrate real-time inference at 26 FPS on STM32H7 and over 1,000 FPS on MAX78000 with its CNN accelerator, enabling practical zero-shot detection on edge devices for the first time.

title: KVSwap: Disk-aware KV Cache Offloading for Long-Context On-device Inference
venue: International Conference on Mobile Systems, Applications, and Services
abstract: Language models (LMs) underpin emerging mobile and embedded AI applications like meeting and video summarization and document analysis, which often require processing multiple long-context inputs. Running an LM locally on-device improves privacy, enables offline use, and reduces cost, but long-context inference quickly hits a \emph{memory capacity wall} as the key-value (KV) cache grows linearly with context length and batch size. Existing KV-cache offloading schemes are designed to transfer cache data from GPU memory to CPU memory; however, they are not suitable for embedded and mobile systems, where the CPU and GPU (or NPU) typically share a unified memory and the non-volatile secondary storage (disk) offers limited I/O bandwidth. We present KVSwap, a software framework tailored for local devices that achieves high memory efficiency while effectively leveraging disk storage. KVSwap stores the full cache on disk, uses highly compact in-memory metadata to predict which entries to preload, overlaps computation with hardware-aware disk access, and orchestrates read patterns to match storage device characteristics. Our evaluation shows that across representative LMs and storage types, KVSwap delivers higher throughput under tight memory budgets while maintaining generation quality over existing KV cache offloading schemes.

title: A Flexible Template for Edge Generative AI With High-Accuracy Accelerated Softmax and GELU
venue: IEEE Journal on Emerging and Selected Topics in Circuits and Systems
abstract: Transformer-based generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) models achieve remarkable results in a wide range of fields, including natural language processing, computer vision, and audio processing. However, this comes at the cost of increased complexity and the need of sophisticated non-linearities such as softmax and GELU. Even if Transformers are computationally dominated by matrix multiplications (MatMul), these non-linearities can become a performance bottleneck, especially if dedicated hardware is used to accelerate MatMul operators. In this work, we introduce a GenAI BFloat16 Transformer acceleration template based on a heterogeneous tightly-coupled cluster containing 256KiB of shared SRAM, 8 general-purpose RISC-V cores, a 24×8 systolic array MatMul accelerator, and a novel accelerator for Transformer softmax, GELU and SiLU nonlinearities: SoftEx. SoftEx introduces an approximate exponentiation algorithm balancing efficiency (121× speedup over glibc’s implementation) with accuracy (mean relative error of 0.14%). In 12 nm technology, SoftEx occupies 0.039 mm2, only 3.22% of the cluster, which achieves an operating frequency of 1.12 GHz. Compared to optimized software running on the RISC-V cores, SoftEx achieves significant improvements, accelerating softmax and GELU computations by up to 10.8× and 5.11×, respectively, while reducing their energy consumption by up to 10.8× and 5.29×. These enhancements translate into a 1.58× increase in throughput (310 GOPS at 0.8 V) and a 1.42× improvement in energy efficiency (1.34 TOPS/W at 0.55 V) on end-to-end ViT inference workloads.

title: Beyond Attention: Efficient 2D Recurrent Mixing for Mobile Vision Backbones
abstract: Mobile and edge devices demand vision backbones that are simultaneously accurate, computationally lightweight, and deployable on hardware accelerators such as the Apple Neural Engine (ANE). Convolutional models are hardware-friendly but struggle to capture longrange spatial dependencies, while Vision Transformers offer global context at the price of quadratic attention complexity. State-space model (SSM) alternatives such as Mamba achieve linear complexity but rely on specialised scan primitives that are absent on mobile neural accelerators, forcing costly CPU fallback. We present Efficient2dGRU, a mobile vision backbone that replaces the attention-based token mixer of EfficientViT with Block2DGRU, a bidirectional 2D recurrent mixer built on the minimal Gated Recurrent Unit (minGRU). The mixing cost is reduced from quadratic O(L2C) to linear O(LC) in the spatial sequence length L, and every primitive in the architecture - 1×1 and 3×3 Conv2d, GroupNorm, element-wise arithmetic, and lower-triangular matrix multiplication - maps directly to ANE-eligible CoreML opcodes. In particular, the standard cumsum/logcumsumexp recurrence is reformulated as a numerically stable parallel prefix scan expressed entirely via lower-triangular matrix multiplications, removing the principal barrier to end-to-end ANE dispatch. On ImageNet-1K, Efficient2dGRU matches the accuracy of its EfficientViT counterpart within 0.5 points across all six model sizes, with the largest variant, Efficient2dGRU-M5, attaining 77.1% top-1 accuracy at 653 MMACs. Measured on an Apple iPhone 15 Pro, Efficient2dGRU-M5 runs at 1.34 ms per image - only 38% slower than EfficientViT-M5 while delivering identical top-1 accuracy with 25% additional compute, and up to 125× faster than MobileMamba models of comparable accuracy. These results demonstrate that a carefully engineered recurrent token mixer can serve as a competitive, hardware-native alternative to both attention and selective-scan mechanisms for real-world mobile vision inference.

title: Design and development of a vulnerability detection framework using artificial intelligence for embedded systems
venue: e-scholar@UOIT (University of Ontario Institute of Technology)
abstract: Embedded systems play a critical role in industrial control, IoT, autonomous systems, and critical infrastructure. However, their widespread adoption introduces security vulnerabilities across three layers: the application layer, the embedded OS layer, and the hardware layer. This thesis presents a comprehensive approach to vulnerability detection and mitigation across these layers, leveraging machine learning, deep learning, and AI-driven solutions. At the application layer, this research focuses on low-level programming applications that control or impact embedded systems, such as firmware, system utilities, and real-time control software. We develop deep learning-based models for automated vulnerability detection, evaluating Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and BERT-based architectures. For the embedded OS layer, we introduced the EVDD dataset (Embedded Vulnerability Detection) to enhance Linux kernel vulnerability detection. Using big data processing, we construct a balanced dataset to improve machine learning models for intrusion detection and OS-level security analysis. Deep neural networks (DNNs) are implemented to detect and mitigate attacks, supporting effective threat detection under resource-constrained environments. At the hardware layer, we investigate vulnerabilities in FPGA based systems, such as bitstream manipulation and HDL coding flaws. We introduce the BitVul-LLM model for detecting FPGA bitstream vulnerabilities, and SecureLLAMA, a transformer-based framework using the FPGAvul dataset to identify hardware security risks. These models automate threat detection and significantly enhance hardware-level security. To improve detection across all layers, we developed an integrated framework using LLama 3, combining our models into a unified AI-driven system. This framework classifies vulnerabilities as hardware, OS-level, or application-level threats, improving precision and response strategies. By correlating vulnerabilities across layers, it enables advanced security assessment, efficient threat mitigation, and proactive defense mechanisms.

title: Photonics-Enabled Edge Processing: A Vision for Near-Sensor Optical Intelligence
venue: ACM Great Lakes Symposium on VLSI (GLSVLSI)
abstract: Edge intelligence is rapidly shifting computation from centralized cloud infrastructure toward the point of data generation. This shift is especially important for visual sensing systems, where continuous streams of high-dimensional pixel data must be converted, stored, transmitted, and processed under strict energy and latency constraints. While processing-in-sensor and processing-near-sensor architectures have reduced data movement, they remain limited by analog-to-digital conversion, memory access, electronic bandwidth, and the difficulty of supporting increasingly complex models near the sensor. This invited paper argues that integrated photonics can provide a new substrate for edge processing by enabling high-bandwidth, low-latency, and naturally parallel analog computation close to the sensing interface. We review the basic principles of photonic computing and discuss how it can be used to realize near-sensor multiply-and-accumulate operations. We then use recent work from our group as representative case studies, including optical in-sensor acceleration, optical near-sensor acceleration with compressive acquisition, near-sensor neuro-symbolic photonic computing, and in-sensor compressed weight retrieval for vision transformers. These examples motivate a broader research agenda in which photonics is not only a fast accelerator for neural operations, but also a system-level enabler for data-centric, energy-aware, and real-time edge intelligence.

title: Decentralized Edge Architecture: Latency Optimization and Hardware Integration for Distributed IoT Nodes
abstract: Background: The prevailing paradigm of digital infrastructure relies on hyper-centralized cloud computing to process data generated by distributed sensors and user endpoints. As the volume of global data generation accelerates—driven by ubiquitous Internet of Things (IoT) devices, autonomous systems, and real-time biometric tracking—this centralized architecture introduces severe latency bottlenecks, bandwidth saturation, and critical data-privacy vulnerabilities. The Hypothesis: We hypothesize that the centralized cloud model is structurally inadequate for next-generation, real-time compute demands. We propose a mandatory transition toward a "Decentralized Edge Architecture," wherein compute logic, machine learning inference, and data processing are localized directly at the IoT node. We argue this topology effectively eliminates cloud-transmission latency and fortifies systemic resilience. Evaluation of the Infrastructure: A network audit reveals that transmitting high-fidelity raw data (such as continuous biometric streams or visual feeds) to centralized data centers introduces round-trip latencies exceeding 100-200 milliseconds, rendering real-time autonomous reactions impossible. Furthermore, the backhaul bandwidth required to sustain continuous transmission from billions of IoT nodes is economically and physically unscalable. Consequences and Strategic Directives: If digital networks do not decentralize, they will face catastrophic data bottlenecks and single-point-of-failure vulnerabilities. Survival of the global IoT network requires aggressive hardware integration of high-efficiency AI accelerators at the edge, the deployment of optimized Small Language Models (SLMs), and a fundamental architectural shift from "cloud-dependent" to "edge-autonomous" systems.

title: An Embedded Hybrid Analog-Digital Training Architecture Based on Phase-Change Memory
Learnable Pulse Accumulation for On-Device Speech Recognition: How Much Attention Do You Need?
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Self-attention scales quadratically with sequence length, limiting transformer-based speech models on edge devices. We introduce the Learnable Pulse Accumulator (LPA), an O(n) replacement that substitutes key-query dot products with learned gating functions: content-dependent rectangular pulses, periodic windows, and position-dependent basis functions. An MSE diagnostic sweep determines per-layer replacement difficulty and ordering. Replacing 8 of 12 wav2vec2-base layers yields 10.61% word error rate (WER) on LibriSpeech test-clean, +7.24 percentage points (pp) over the 3.37% baseline, with 3.27x speedup at 120s audio on Apple M4 Pro via an optimized MLX inference path. Cross-domain validation on SepFormer speech enhancement shows all 16 intra-chunk attention layers can be replaced without collapse, suggesting the depth wall arises from linguistic computation rather than an LPA limitation. LPA's near-binary gates at inference enable dense GPU computation with no CPU-GPU synchronization, and all operations map to mobile neural accelerators.

title: Editorial: Talking fabrics – a new era in autonomous AI textile wearable (AITW) technology
venue: International Journal of Clothing Science and Technology
abstract: In a world where technology constantly transforms the boundaries of possibility, we find ourselves at the intersection of a quiet but powerful revolution: the fusion of artificial intelligence (AI) with the fabrics that we wear as garments. This remarkable evolution in wearable technology is not simply a step forward but a giant leap into an era where our clothing becomes an extension of our own cognitive experience. In fact, it provides what AI needs to go from “chatting unaware of the user” to becoming more intelligent by understanding the user's physical and environmental conditions and hence providing “contextual understanding”, which is the next most important requirement in AI's quest to achieve large action models (LAM) for higher intelligence. The research presented here introduces this new frontier of “AI textiles (AIT).”The notion of intelligent textiles isn't new. Increasingly, fabrics are considered organic beings, capable of understanding and reacting to human conditions and environment (Stylios, 2020). What makes this work by Aliyana and Stylios exciting is its tangible manifestation of that vision. AI wearables (AITW) is a prime example of the realm of autonomous cognitive ability. An AIT is a system that listens, monitors and measures processes and converses with its wearer. Powered by self-harvested energy through triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) embedded in the textile, an AIT monitors biomechanical data (movement, temperature, breathing, heart rate, resistivity, touch, etc.), turns that data into contextual information so that the communication between the BOT and the user is moving to a higher level of AI than at present. By embedding AI in a fabric that responds to real-time data, AIT transcends the traditional role of wearables. It actively participates in all activities of its wearer, offering personalized feedback, from gait analysis through voice interaction and is responsive to the user's real-world needs. We can call these Autonomous Intelligent Agents (AIAs) or Autonomous Intelligent Copilots (AICs). They understand not just what the user says, but also the context, intent and situational background. They personalize responses and actions based on user history, preferences and real-time data. Make autonomous decisions and take proactive steps to help or alert the user and continuously learn and adapt, becoming more effective over time, rather than simply reacting to commands, as bots do at present. These autonomous agents will be the textile or the wearable garment itself, hence calling them AITAs or AITWAs, respectively.The evolution from passive question-answering AI like ChatGPT to advanced AAI represents a significant leap toward higher intelligence. This shift transforms AI from a reactive tool into an autonomous, proactive system capable of complex reasoning, decision-making and real-world action. Let us break down the reasons why and how this advancement occurs. This is a leap in intelligence because AIA surpasses models like ChatGPT in three critical dimensions: firstly, in autonomy and proactivity; unlike ChatGPT, which waits for user prompts, AIA independently initiates actions, sets goals and adapts strategies based on environmental data (e.g. user habits, sensor inputs, etc). An example might be an AIA monitoring a user's health metrics might proactively adjust room temperature or suggest rest without being asked. Secondly, in contextual depth and memory, ChatGPT resets context between interactions, while AIAs maintain long-term memory, retaining user preferences, historical data and environmental states to inform decisions. This enables nuanced personalization, such as refining recommendations based on past behaviour. Thirdly, in task execution and integration, AIAs integrate with external systems (APIs and IoT devices) to execute multi-step workflows like booking travel or controlling smart homes far beyond ChatGPT's text-based responses. They solve complex problems by analysing real-time data (e.g. optimizing logistics routes) (Constantino, 2025; Nahavandi et al., 2022).This advancement is achieved because AIA leverages four technical innovations to enable higher intelligence:Therefore, as we can see, AITs mark a paradigm shift by merging contextual awareness, autonomous decision-making and real-world action, transforming AI from a conversational partner into an intelligent collaborator. This is achieved through architectures that emulate human-like reasoning, continuous learning and seamless system integration, enabling agents to tackle dynamic, multifaceted challenges that passive models cannot. Table 1 shows a comparison between a chatbot like ChatGPT and AIT agents.Networked AITA/AITW agents' communication is where agents share contextual data from textile wearables about users during interactions, which could transform how humans connect by making conversations more informed, empathetic and efficient. This system would function like an advanced social layer over platforms (e.g. Facebook, X and Instagram), but with explicit user consent and real-time data exchange between AIAs, see Figure 1. Below, we analyse its potential to enhance interactions, its broader effects and key regulatory considerations.As we have discussed, textiles provide the ability of AIA to have continuous contextual enrichment and become AIA themselves as AITAs. AITAs could share non-sensitive, user-approved context (e.g. “Alex just returned from Japan” or “Sam prefers video calls over texts”) before or during conversations. This allows participants to tailor discussions to shared interests or recent events, fostering deeper engagement. Textiles worn by users can provide AI agents the ability of “proactive assistance”; agents might alert users to “potential sensitivities” (e.g. “avoid discussing travel: Maya's flight was cancelled today”) or suggest “conversation starters” based on mutual hobbies, reducing social friction and building rapport textiles will also provide “efficiency in networking”; for professional settings, agents could exchange role-specific backgrounds (e.g. “Taylor's expertise: IoT security”), enabling more focused and productive collaborations. In fact, these AI agents are the AITAs/AITGAs themselves.It is inevitable that there are incredibly positive effects with this new technical breakthrough but also negative effects, which will need mitigation. A welcome positive effect is the deeper personalization, in which conversations feel more relevant and empathetic, as agents provide real-time context about mood, preferences or milestones (South et al., 2025; IBM, 2024). But privacy could be eroded by oversharing without granular consent, exposing sensitive traits (e.g. health status) or enabling manipulation. Another welcome aspect is the build-up of stronger relationships, because shared context fosters trust and common ground, mimicking the intuition of close friendships, but at the same time, users may feel social pressure and might alter behaviour if aware they're being “analysed,” leading to inauthentic interactions, which may be a negative effect. The technology can have another positive effect in conflict reduction because agents could flag incompatible communication styles (e.g. “Jamal dislikes interruptions”) to prevent misunderstandings (South et al., 2025). However, this feature also risks amplifying bias if agents rely on incomplete data, reinforce stereotypes or inherit algorithmic biases that may influence user perceptions.As textile wearable garments can provide contextual-based data from the wearer to enable the AI agents to become more intelligent, personal and effective, as we have seen, several regulatory and ethical constraints must be put in place; for example, the wearer should have a “consent-first design” where the user must explicitly opt into data sharing per interaction, with options to limit context (e.g. “share my hobbies but not my location”). Regulations like GDPR and the EU AI Act mandate this granular control. Then the question of “transparency”, in which agents should disclose when/why context is shared (e.g. “Based on your LinkedIn, I suggested your startup experience”) to maintain trust. And very importantly, the insurance of “human oversight”, in which high-stakes scenarios (e.g. conflict mediation) should require human review to override agent suggestions, aligns with GDPR's Article 2 “right to explanation” (European Union, 2016; UK Government, 2018). In consequence, AI agent/textile wearable networking could make human interactions more intuitive and meaningful by leveraging contextual data, turning superficial chats into enriched exchanges. However, this hinges on strict consent protocols, transparent data usage and bias mitigation to avoid privacy harms or social manipulation. While regulation (like the EU AI Act) is evolving to address these risks, the priority remains for user autonomy: ensuring agents enhance, not dictate, human connection (European Union, 2024).The future will involve textile wearables carrying AI-enabled devices with nano chips for local processing while leveraging larger cloud-based models, creating a hybrid architecture optimized for performance, privacy and efficiency. This approach aligns with the evolution of AIA (specifically edge AI agents), which combine autonomy, contextual awareness and distributed intelligence. In this case, AIGA became Edge AIGAs. These wearables are already autonomous in terms of energy and sensing by virtue of their yarns and fabric structures, and ideally, it will be their battery-free provision to be maintained so that their energy harvesting ability will be sufficient to make the AI nano chips for local processing work battery-free. Below is a breakdown of how this works:Let us discuss how this can work in a real end-use scenario.So, this is a real scenario which benefits from a textile enabling contextual understanding by sensing physiological and environmental data from the wearer and so lifting the intelligence of the agent to edge, which stays locally in the wearable textile system, facilitated by a nano chip in the textile and the cloud-based agent as seen in Table 2.There is an interesting and more sustainable AI industry in a future outlook based on the above considerations, such as 5 G/IoT Synergy, where there will be a faster edge-cloud synchronization for complex tasks (e.g. AR-assisted surgery) (MarketsandMarkets, 2024). Then, self-learning wearables (SLW) embedded with nano chips will locally retrain models using federated learning, reducing cloud dependence (Lyzr, 2024). This will make wearable textile garments truly autonomous edge agents on their own right, increasing the need for better implementation of ethical guardrails by easier-to-administer user-controlled consent layers (e.g. “Share heart data only for emergency alerts”) (MIT Computing, 2024; MarketsandMarkets, 2024). Therefore, carrying AI-enabled wearables with nano chips is essential for real-time responsiveness and privacy, while cloud-based models handle deeper intelligence. AI agents bridge these layers, creating a cohesive, efficient system where edge devices act as autonomous “first responders” and the cloud serves as a “strategic brain.” This architecture will dominate future tech and will change our lives forever. It is expected to replace Google, Facebook, Yahoo, X and Instagram. To achieve an advanced AIA capable of context awareness, personalization, decision-making and proactive assistance, the hardware and software must integrate edge-device efficiency with cloud-scale intelligence. Below is a summary of requirements based on current technological advancements:Edge textile wearables/IoT will need ultra-low-power processors, i.e., nano-chips like NeuroSense (consuming <100 µW) for real-time sensor data processing (e.g. motion), especially since their power (TENG) will have to be provided by the movement generated in the textile by the wearer (Aliyana et al., 2024). Sensing will be inherent to the textile-based wearable, and it will depend on the type of fibres the textile is made of. Finally, connectivity will be based on Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE), or 5G RedCap/NB-IoT will be employed to ensure minimal energy consumption during cloud communication (NeuroSense, 2024). In contrast, cloud infrastructure will rely on high-performance accelerators, such as NVIDIA H200 SXM, H100 SXM, TPUs and FPGAs, for training large AI models and executing complex inference tasks. In contrast, the cloud infrastructure will rely on high-performance accelerators, such as GPUs (NVIDIA H200 SXM and H1oo SXM, TPUs and FPGAs), for training large AI models and complex inference tasks. These chips consume hundreds of watts of power and require robust power delivery and thermal management systems. Scalable, high-throughput storage using NVMe SSDs will also be essential for rapid access to large datasets during training and retrieval. While edge devices focus on energy-efficient sensing and minimal computation, cloud systems are optimized for performance, throughput and large-scale model hosting, reinforcing the distributed nature of modern AI-powered wearables.Edge Software, which is based on the textile wearable agent, stays local within the nano chip-based system by means of tiny ML frameworks, such as TensorFlow Lite or Edge Impulse, for deploying lightweight models on wearables (Latent AI, 2024). The need for a real-time OS, optimized for low-latency textile wearable sensing data processing and local decision-making. And importantly, federated learning enables on-device model updates without raw data leaving the device (Latent AI, 2024; Zilliz, 2024). Cloud software must perform AI orchestration so that platforms like SmythOS or Latent AI will be used to manage agent workflows, versioning and scaling (Milvus, 2024). MLOps tools will be used for continuous deployment, monitoring and updating of edge models (e.g. latent AI's telemetry) (Zilliz, 2024). And finally, facilitate APIs/services for cloud-based AI APIs (e.g., Azure Cognitive Services) for complex tasks like NLP. So, if we were to look at this hybrid architecture workflow, it would consist of the following layers:For this hybrid architecture workflow, we will need the following development requirements: hardware with ≥8 GB RAM, multi-core processors (Intel i5+/AMD Ryzen) and 20 GB + storage for testing wearable apps. And tools like SDKs for target platforms (Android/iOS), BLE debuggers and AI optimization suites. In essence, the future demands capable, durable and comfortable textile wearables; hardware that balances ultra-low-power edge processing with cloud-scale computation, coupled with software that enables seamless, privacy-preserving intelligence across this hybrid architecture (Nahavandi et al., 2022; Shajari et al., 2023; EEJournal, 2024; Google Cloud, 2024).
